name: Elastic N.V. (formerly Elasticsearch BV)
origin_detail: Shay Banon wrote Compass (2004) and released Elasticsearch, a rewrite, as Apache-2.0 open source in February 2010. He co-founded the company with Steven Schuurman, Uri Boness and Simon Willnauer in Amsterdam in 2012. Dutch N.V. with major US operations (San Francisco/Mountain View) and an NYSE listing (ESTC), so it is US-relevant despite the Dutch domicile.
openness_notes: Elasticsearch and Kibana were Apache-2.0 from 2010; the company later sold proprietary features (X-Pack) and Elastic Cloud (open core). In early 2021 (from 7.11) the free code moved to a dual SSPL / Elastic License 2.0 choice, which is not OSI-approved (level 1). On 2024-08-29 Elastic added AGPL-3.0 as a third option, so the free code is OSI open source again while paid features stay proprietary: current level 2.

license_history.note: Announced 2024-08-29, in place before 8.16 GA; existing SSPL/ELv2 users unaffected.

relicensing_events.fork: OpenSearch (and OpenSearch Dashboards), forked from Elasticsearch/Kibana 7.10.2, first released April 2021
relicensing_events.fork_backer: AWS; transferred on 2024-09-16 to the OpenSearch Software Foundation (Linux Foundation) with premier members AWS, SAP, Uber and general members incl. Aiven, Atlassian, Canonical, DigitalOcean, NetApp Instaclustr
relicensing_events.outcome_note: AWS announced the fork about a week after Elastic's change. By the foundation's one-year mark (Aug 2025) OpenSearch reported downloads up 78% year-on-year, past 1 billion in total.

Partial reversal: OSI-approved licence restored for the free tier. Commentators (The New Stack, OpenUK via ITPro) questioned whether trust would return and asked whether OpenSearch's success proved that forking works.

exit_events.note: Priced 2018-10-04 at $36 (above a raised $33-35 range; original $26-29), 7M shares, $252M raised; closed day one at $70, a market cap of almost $4.9B. Banon: 'we didn't really IPO to raise money'.

risk_events: 2021-01: Relicense to SSPL/ELv2; AWS forked Elasticsearch and Kibana as Apache-2.0 OpenSearch
2024-09-16: OpenSearch moved to a neutral Linux Foundation foundation with AWS, SAP and Uber as premier members
2024-08-29: Partial reversal to AGPL, met with community scepticism about long-term commitment
Market cap volatile: roughly $6.7B-$9.0B in July-August 2026 snapshots vs ~$10.2B on 2026-10-30
robustness: Single-vendor control of Elasticsearch; no foundation. A well-funded, foundation-governed fork (OpenSearch) now competes head-on, so customers have an exit path. Financially solid: FY2026 revenue $1.739B (+17%), non-GAAP operating margin 16.4%, though GAAP operating loss of $33M; Q2 FY2027 revenue $496M (+17%).
physical_science_relevance: Elasticsearch/OpenSearch are common backbones for log, telemetry and literature search in research infrastructure.
openness_effect_assessment: Apache licensing made Elasticsearch the default search engine and supported a $4.9B first-day IPO valuation in 2018. Closing to SSPL/ELv2 in 2021 did not hurt revenue growth much (revenue reached $1.74B in FY2026), but it triggered the most successful hyperscaler fork in this group: OpenSearch, now at the Linux Foundation with over a billion downloads. Elastic's 2024 AGPL return shows the company judged the fork and the lost open-source label to be costlier than the protection SSPL gave.
key_takeaway: Elastic is the canonical relicense-fork-reversal story. Closing the licence protected Elastic Cloud from AWS resale, but it handed AWS the moral high ground and a permanent, foundation-governed fork that splits the ecosystem. Three years later Elastic re-added an OSI licence (AGPL), keeping SSPL/ELv2 alongside. The company stayed public and growing throughout, so the closing was not fatal, but it permanently lost sole control of the search-engine standard it created.
